title: Digital companies are expanding connectivity and AI capacity while emissions, electricity demand, and climate-accountability gaps remain material
source_unit: International Telecommunication Union and World Benchmarking Alliance, Greening Digital Companies 2026: Monitoring Emissions and Climate Commitments
geography: 200 digital companies worldwide assessed on greenhouse-gas emissions, energy consumption, climate commitments, and transition plans

companies_assessed.unit: digital companies covered by the report

scope_coverage.value: the assessment examines Scope 1, Scope 2, and Scope 3 greenhouse-gas emissions

commitment_question.value: climate commitments and transition plans are assessed alongside reported emissions and energy use

observations.method: ITU and World Benchmarking Alliance comparative assessment of digital companies' emissions, energy, climate targets, and transition-plan disclosures.
observations.uncertainty: Company disclosures and benchmarking criteria do not capture all supply-chain effects, hidden energy use, local impacts, or whether commitments are implemented and additional.
observations.subgroup: Digital firms, data-center operators, network providers, workers, investors, regulators, communities near infrastructure, and users dependent on digital services.
observations.counterinterpretation: Transparent measurement and credible transition plans can accelerate clean-energy procurement, efficiency, innovation, and accountability across digital value chains.

denominator.unit: reporting digital companies with disclosed electricity consumption data

reporting_companies.unit: companies reporting electricity consumption in the assessment

electricity_consumption.unit: terawatt-hours of electricity consumed in 2024 by reporting companies

global_share.unit: approximately percent of global electricity consumption represented by the reported 2024 total

growth_pressure.value: AI and digital expansion can increase electricity demand even as firms pursue renewable electricity and efficiency

observations.method: ITU and WBA aggregation of company-reported electricity consumption and comparison with global electricity use.
observations.uncertainty: The total covers reporting companies, not the whole digital sector; accounting boundaries, estimates, procurement contracts, and operational versus embodied energy differ across firms.
observations.subgroup: Data-center communities, electricity systems, utilities, digital workers, users, investors, and regions hosting high-load infrastructure.
observations.counterinterpretation: Digital services can reduce travel, improve energy management, and support climate monitoring, while demand growth and rebound effects may offset efficiency gains.

observations.period: 2026; AI, climate action, and environmental costs

denominator.unit: digital-sector AI, energy, emissions, and climate-transition frame

benefit_channel.value: AI can support climate action through energy optimization, renewable forecasting, and efficiency gains

cost_channel.value: AI also carries environmental costs through growing computation, electricity demand, hardware, and supply chains

net_effect_question.value: the net climate effect depends on deployment scale, rebound, energy sources, hardware lifecycles, and credible measurement

observations.method: ITU and WBA synthesis of digital-company environmental metrics and transition commitments.
observations.uncertainty: The report does not estimate a single global net effect of AI on emissions or prove that any company's AI use creates additional climate benefits.
observations.subgroup: AI developers, cloud and data-center firms, utilities, technology users, climate agencies, workers, and communities exposed to energy or material demand.
observations.counterinterpretation: AI applications may produce substantial avoided emissions in some sectors, but avoided-emissions claims require transparent baselines and cannot substitute for direct reductions.

observations.period: 2026; digital transition, public capacity, and distributed exposure

denominator.unit: digital-company governance, infrastructure, climate, market, and public-accountability frame

infrastructure_tradeoff.value: digital infrastructure is simultaneously a service platform, an energy load, a material system, and a source of market power

accountability_surface.value: disclosure, transition planning, procurement, regulation, and community participation determine who bears digital growth costs and who receives benefits

policy_question.value: the open question is whether digital expansion aligns private growth with public climate and infrastructure capacity

observations.method: Program-level synthesis linking the ITU/WBA company assessment to energy, infrastructure, market power, and public-systems themes.
observations.uncertainty: This is an analytical bridge, not a causal estimate from the report; company-level disclosure cannot establish community-level distribution or political legitimacy.
observations.subgroup: Digital firms, communities, regulators, utilities, consumers, workers, investors, and public infrastructure systems.
observations.counterinterpretation: Strong public standards and competition can make digital growth compatible with decarbonization, affordability, resilience, and shared value.

related_sources.claim: ITU ICT Development Index 2026 provides complementary evidence on the expansion and uneven quality of digital connectivity.
Google's 2026 Environmental Report provides a company-level comparator for clean-energy procurement, electricity demand, and operational emissions.

boundary: This record adds a digital-company climate, energy, emissions, transition-plan, and public-accountability route. It uses company comparisons and disclosed aggregates, not user-level behavior, causal AI climate effects, complete lifecycle accounting, or proof that renewable procurement eliminates local environmental burdens.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official ITU/WBA Greening Digital Companies 2026 materials were reviewed for 200-company coverage, Scope 1-3 emissions, 163-company electricity reporting, 494 TWh of 2024 consumption, the approximate global share, and AI climate benefits and costs.
